ety.text: Likely from dialectal dodge, dod, dodd (“to jog, trudge along, totter", also "to jerk, jig”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from unrecorded Middle English *dodden, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *dud- (“to move”), related to Old English dydrian, dyderian (“to delude, deceive”), Middle English dideren (“to tremble, quake, shiver”), English dodder, Norwegian dudra (“to tremble”).

senses.d: To avoid (something) by moving suddenly out of the way.
ex: He dodged traffic crossing the street.
The politician dodged the question with a meaningless reply.

senses.d: To go, or cause to go, hither and thither.
To make an area of an image lighter (when processing photographs in a darkroom, this is accomplished by decreasing the exposure of that area to light).
To follow by dodging, or suddenly shifting from place to place.
ex: "I had a notion he was dodging me all the way I came, for I saw him just behind me, turn which way I would."
A speck, a mist, a shape, I wist! / And still it neared and neared: / As if it dodged a water-sprite, / It plunged and tacked and veered.

senses.d: A trick, evasion or wile. (Now mainly in the expression tax dodge.)
ex: The dodges of women beat all comprehension; and I am sure she wouldn’t let the lad off so easily, if she had not some other scheme on hand.
“Ain't this a rum go? This is a queer sort of dodge for lighting the streets.”
In the marketing dodge, that is known as rub-off.

grp.label: to avoid by moving out of the way
photography: to make lighter (to decrease the exposure of an area of a photo)

fr:contourner.gl: to circumvent, to bypass, to skirt around

ety.text: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contornāre, from cum and tornāre. Also con- + tourner.
Inherited from Middle French esquiver (“to escape”), from Spanish esquivar (“to avoid, reject, elude”), itself from Old French eschiver from Proto-West Germanic *skiuhan, if not formed from esquivo.

it:schivare.gl: to dodge, sidestep, avoid, or evade

ety.text: Borrowed from Old French eschiver (“to escape, avoid”).
From s- (“intensifying prefix”) + cansare (from Latin campsāre (“to turn or sail around a place”), related to Ancient Greek κάμπτω (kámptō, “to turn”)).

es:esquivar.gl: to dodge, to duck, to evade

ety.text: From esquivo + -ar. Cognate with English eschew, Old High German sciuhen (“to frighten, make fearful”), and Dutch schuwen (“to caution”). More at shy.

chain.g: to finish play, cease to sport

it:eludere.gl: to evade, to elude, to dodge, to sidestep
